analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax.
analysis.headline: The bill to replace the federal income tax with a 23% national sales tax drew 54 cosponsors but never got a hearing or vote in the House Ways and Means Committee, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the entire federal income tax, the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replaced them with a 23% national sales tax on nearly everything people buy, collected mostly by the states. Monthly rebates would offset the tax up to the poverty level for registered families. Because high-income households save and invest much of their money while working families spend nearly all of theirs, the switch would have shifted the tax burden toward people who spend what they earn and away from wealth.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households and the wealthiest families gain the most: their income taxes, capital gains and dividend taxes, and estate and gift taxes would be repealed entirely, and untaxed savings and investment would escape tax altogether. Taxpayers of all incomes would gain the end of filing income tax returns. Families below the poverty line would be made whole on the sales tax through the monthly rebate, but families just above it would pay the full tax on everything they buy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, investors, and large estates

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal income tax, including taxes on wages, capital gains, and dividends, ending income tax filing for individuals and businesses [S2][S3].
Repeals the Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, replacing that funding with a portion of the sales tax (a 14.91% general revenue rate plus Social Security and Medicare rates) [S2][S3].
Repeals the federal estate and gift taxes entirely, eliminating the tax on inherited wealth [S2][S3].
Abolishes the Internal Revenue Service as an income tax collector, with the new sales tax administered primarily by state tax agencies for a 0.25% fee [S2][S3].

Provides a monthly 'family consumption allowance' rebate equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty level for each registered family, protecting households up to the poverty line from the sales tax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Working households that spend most or all of their income would pay the 23% sales tax on essentially every purchase, while households able to save and invest large shares of their income would see most of their money go untaxed. The estate tax repeal would concentrate the benefit on the largest inheritances. Retailers would bear new collection and remittance duties (partially compensated by an administrative credit), and state governments would take on federal tax collection.
analysis.who_pays_short: Working families who spend what they earn

drawbacks.text: A consumption tax falls hardest on people who spend all of their income; the rebate offsets the tax only up to the poverty level, so working families above it would pay the full 23% on every purchase while wealthier households' savings and investment income would go untaxed [S3].

Repealing the estate and gift tax directly benefits the wealthiest estates, and repealing income tax on investment returns means large accumulated wealth would never be taxed under the new system [S2][S3].

The stated 23% rate is tax-inclusive; measured the way state sales taxes are quoted, it is roughly a 30% addition to the price of goods and services, and the rate could rise in later years because it is set by formula [S3].

Social Security and Medicare would no longer be funded by dedicated payroll taxes but from general sales tax revenue, ending the link between contributions and benefits and putting retirement funding at the mercy of annual consumption levels and future rate-setting [S2][S3].
Families would have to register annually with the government, listing household members and Social Security numbers, to keep receiving the rebate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real simplicity gains and a genuine anti-poverty rebate, but its core design moves the tax burden from income and wealth onto consumption. For a typical working family, the sales tax it pays on everything it buys would likely exceed the income and payroll taxes it no longer pays, while the largest gains go to high earners and to estates that would no longer pay any tax. Honest supporters would acknowledge the regressive shift; the design partially offsets it at the poverty line but does nothing above it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or markup or a floor vote, and expired when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. John Linder introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2003 on January 7, 2003, with Rep. Collin Peterson of Minnesota as the other original sponsor [S3][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means on the day of introduction; that was the only committee action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill accumulated 54 cosponsors, 52 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S4].
The sponsor gave introductory remarks on the House floor more than a year later, on May 5, 2004, but the bill still received no committee consideration [S5].
No action followed after that; the bill sat in committee until the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and it died without ever reaching the House floor [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing tax system stayed in place. Working households that spend most of their income were spared the shift to a consumption tax, and it was never tested whether the promised rebates and rate would hold up in practice. The bill's supporters lost another Congress; the beneficiaries of its repeal of income and estate taxes had to keep waiting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Working households spared a consumption tax shift

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 52 of the 54 cosponsors were Republicans, with only 2 Democrats, and no committee or floor action ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill repeals income tax on investment returns and abolishes the estate and gift tax, while shifting the revenue burden onto consumption. Because the wealthy save a large share of their income, their effective tax rate would fall sharply while working households' would rise.
Administering states would collect the federal sales tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, giving them a new revenue stream and a permanent role collecting federal taxes.

Sellers would have to register, collect, and remit the tax, but would receive an administrative credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted (capped at 20% of tax due), compensating many smaller sellers for the compliance burden.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax would eliminate the compliance work the income tax system generates, a loss for the industry that coincides with taxpayers no longer needing to file.
